title: Episode 267: Amelia Earhart: The Queen of the Air, the Transatlantic Solo, and the Mystery of Howland Island
description:
The daring, trailblazing, and legendary life of Amelia Earhart: the pioneering Kansas aviator who shattered gender barriers to become the world's most famous woman pilot. First crossing the Atlantic in 1928 as a passenger aboard the Friendship, Earhart silenced critics in May 1932 by flying solo across the treacherous North Atlantic in her bright red Lockheed Vega monoplane, becoming the first woman to conquer the ocean alone. Co-founding the Ninety-Nines organization for female aviators, breaking altitude and speed records, and championing women's independence, Earhart embarked on an audacious twenty-nine-thousand-mile equatorial circumnavigation of the globe in 1937 with navigator Fred Noonan. Vanishing into the vast Pacific expanse near Howland Island, Earhart remains an eternal symbol of courage, freedom, and the boundless human spirit.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Top 50 Famous Non-President Americans series celebrates the fearless queen of the clouds: the Kansas pioneer who broke through the glass ceiling of aviation and inspired women across the globe to claim the sky. Here is George with the life of Amelia Earhart.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE TOMBOY OF ATCHISON: 1897 TO 1920
Born in July 1897 in the gracious Victorian home of her affluent grandparents overlooking the Missouri River in Atchison, Kansas, Amelia Mary Earhart was a fiercely independent, adventurous tomboy from her earliest childhood. While Victorian society dictated that young girls wear ruffled dresses and play with porcelain dolls, Amelia climbed apple trees, hunted rats with a twenty-two-caliber rifle, and constructed a homemade roller-coaster track off the roof of her family's tool shed, crashing to the dirt in a wooden soapbox and declaring with bloody knees: 'Oh, it felt like flying!' During World War I, while visiting her sister in Toronto, Canada, Amelia was deeply moved by the sight of wounded Canadian soldiers returning from the Western Front, volunteering as a nurse's aide at the Spadina Military Hospital, where she spent hours listening to the exploits of Royal Flying Corps pursuit pilots. In December 1920, while attending a Long Beach air meet in California with her father, Amelia paid ten dollars for a ten-minute flight with World War I pilot Frank Hawks. As the biplane soared two or three hundred feet above the Pacific coast, Amelia experienced an electrifying revelation that altered the course of her life: 'As soon as we left the ground, I knew I myself had to fly.'  Young Amelia's tomboy independence in Atchison defied the rigid gender conventions of Victorian America, fostering her fearless belief that women were capable of any physical endeavor. Her compassionate nursing service in Toronto military hospitals during the First World War gave her a firsthand glimpse into the courage and fragile mortality of young aviators.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE CANARY AND THE FRIENDSHIP FLIGHT: 1921 TO 1928
Taking flying lessons from pioneer woman aviator Neta Snook at Kinner Field, Amelia cropped her brown hair short and slept in a new leather flight jacket for three nights to give it a weathered, veteran appearance. Purchasing an experimental, bright yellow Kinner Airster biplane nicknamed 'The Canary', twenty-five-year-old Earhart set a world altitude record for female pilots in 1922 by climbing to fourteen thousand feet. Working as a social worker at Denison House settlement home in Boston, Amelia received a life-altering telephone call in April 1928: publisher and public relations genius George Palmer Putnam invited her to become the first woman to cross the Atlantic Ocean by air. On June 17, 1928, pilot Wilmer Stultz and mechanic Lou Gordon flew the triple-engine Fokker floatplane Friendship across the Atlantic from Newfoundland to Wales, with Amelia keeping the flight logbook. Greeted with rapturous ticker-tape parades in New York and dubbed 'Lady Lindy' for her striking physical resemblance to Charles Lindbergh, Amelia was deeply embarrassed by the adulation, frankly telling reporters: 'Stultz did all the flying—had to. I was just baggage, like a sack of potatoes. Maybe someday I'll try it alone.'  Her bright yellow Kinner Airster biplane, 'The Canary', was purchased through her own earnings as a truck driver and telephone company clerk, demonstrating her fierce self-reliance. The Friendship flight of 1928 made Amelia an overnight global symbol of modern womanhood, though she steadfastly refused to take unearned credit for the piloting.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE RED VEGA AND THE SOLO ATLANTIC CROSSING: MAY 1932
Four years later, Amelia Earhart made good on her promise. On the evening of May 20, 1932—the exact fifth anniversary of Charles Lindbergh's flight—thirty-four-year-old Earhart climbed into the cockpit of her modified, bright red Lockheed 5B Vega monoplane at Harbour Grace, Newfoundland. Armed with only a thermos of hot tomato soup, smelling salts, and a single can of tomato juice, she took off alone into the Atlantic night toward Paris. The fifteen-hour crossing was a terrifying trial: four hours into the flight, her altimeter failed, leaving her blind to her height above the dark waves. Flying into a ferocious thunderstorm, severe icing coated the red wings, sending the plane into a sickening, three-thousand-foot uncontrolled spin toward the sea, recovering barely fifty feet above the white-capped ocean. To compound the danger, a cracked manifold broke, shooting blue exhaust flames into the cockpit, while gasoline began dripping down her neck from a broken reserve fuel line. Realizing that Paris was impossible, Earhart altered course toward the nearest land: at one-thirty PM on May 21, she touched down in a pasture at Culmore, near Derry in Northern Ireland, scattering cows. A farmer ran out shouting: 'Have you flown far?' Amelia replied with a grin: 'From America!' She was the first woman —and only the second person in history—to fly solo across the Atlantic.  The solo Atlantic crossing in the red Lockheed Vega was an extraordinary feat of raw flying skill, battling manifold fires, broken instruments, and severe wing icing through an ocean tempest. Her humble arrival in a Northern Ireland cow pasture underscored her unpretentious character, transforming an emergency landing into an immortal moment of international warmth.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE NINETY-NINES AND THE PACIFIC SOLO: 1932 TO 1935
Amelia Earhart used her immense international celebrity to dismantle the deeply entrenched sexism of the aviation industry. In 1929, she co-founded the Ninety-Nines—an international organization of ninety-nine licensed women pilots—serving as its first president and lobbying tirelessly for female commercial pilot licenses and military transport recognition. Having married George Palmer Putnam in 1931 under an unconventional, egalitarian marriage pact in which she demanded complete personal independence and refused to be bound by traditional domestic expectations, Amelia continued breaking aviation barriers. In January 1935, Earhart became the first pilot of any gender to fly solo across the treacherous twenty-four-hundred-mile expanse of the Pacific Ocean between Honolulu, Hawaii, and Oakland, California, listening to civilian radio broadcasts of the Metropolitan Opera to verify her course through the night. Months later, she flew solo non-stop from Los Angeles to Mexico City, and from Mexico City to New York, winning the National Geographic Society's Special Gold Medal presented by President Herbert Hoover.  The founding of the Ninety-Nines established a vital support network for female aviators, opening commercial flying careers and aeronautical engineering to future generations of women. Her marriage agreement with George Putnam championed modern partnership over traditional subordination, insisting on her right to pursue professional adventure on her own terms.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE WORLD FLIGHT AND THE FLYING LABORATORY: 1937
As she approached her fortieth birthday, Amelia planned her crowning aviation achievement: circumnavigating the globe as close to the equator as possible—a colossal twenty-nine-thousand-mile odyssey that had never been attempted. Funded by Purdue University, where Earhart served as a visiting counselor for women careers, Lockheed manufactured a custom Model 10E Electra: an all-metal, twin-engine monoplane nicknamed the 'Flying Laboratory', outfitted with massive auxiliary fuselage fuel tanks holding twelve hundred gallons of gasoline and advanced Hamilton Standard variable-pitch propellers. After an initial westward attempt in March 1937 ended in a disastrous ground-loop crash on takeoff from Honolulu that tore off the landing gear, Earhart and Putnam rebuilt the plane. Reversing course to fly eastward due to seasonal global weather patterns, Amelia departed Miami on June 1, 1937, accompanied by master maritime celestial navigator Fred Noonan. Over the next thirty days, Earhart and Noonan flew twenty-two thousand miles across South America, Africa, India, and Southeast Asia, arriving safely in Lae, New Guinea, on June 29, having completed three-quarters of the global journey.  The twin-engine Lockheed Electra represented the cutting edge of 1930s aviation engineering, customized with auxiliary fuel tanks to conquer the vast distances of the equatorial globe. The twenty-two-thousand-mile journey across South America, Africa, and Asia demonstrated Earhart and Noonan's exceptional navigational skill through extreme equatorial weather.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE LAST HOP: LAE TO HOWLAND ISLAND: JULY 2, 1937
On the morning of July 2, 1937, the twin-engine Electra stood at the end of the unpaved coastal runway at Lae, heavy with eleven hundred gallons of fuel. Ahead lay the most hazardous, terrifying leg of the entire circumnavigation: a twenty-five-hundred-and-fifty-six-mile flight across the featureless expanse of the central Pacific to Howland Island—a tiny, uninhabited coral sandbar measuring barely one and a half miles long and half a mile wide. To guide the plane down, the United States Coast Guard cutter Itasca was anchored offshore at Howland, emitting radio homing signals. Taking off at midnight UTC, Earhart faced head winds and dense Pacific cloud banks that prevented Noonan from taking celestial star sights with his octant. At seven-forty-two AM on July 2, the Itasca's radio room picked up Earhart's anxious, static-crackle voice: 'We must be on you, but cannot see you—but gas is running low. Been unable to reach you by radio. We are flying at one thousand feet.' At eight-forty-three AM, Earhart sent her final, desperate confirmed transmission: 'We are on the line 157 337... We are running on line north and south.' Then, the Pacific fell silent.  The tragic final transmission picked up by the Coast Guard cutter Itasca reflected the terrifying reality of hunting for a tiny coral speck in the infinite expanse of the Pacific Ocean. Despite extensive modern sonar mapping and archaeological searches, the mystery of Howland Island has kept its secret, preserving Amelia's legend in the mists of the Pacific.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE VANISHED QUEEN OF THE CLOUDS: THE IMMORTAL SPIRIT
President Franklin D. Roosevelt immediately authorized the largest maritime search in naval history: nine naval warships, sixty-six aircraft, and over four thousand sailors scoured two hundred and fifty thousand square miles of open ocean for sixteen days, finding no trace of the Electra or its crew. On July 19, 1937, the Navy officially abandoned the search. While theories regarding her disappearance have proliferated for nearly a century—ranging from crashing and sinking in the eighteen-thousand-foot depths of the Pacific trench, to marooning and dying on the coral atoll of Gardner Island (Nikumaroro), to capture by Japanese military forces—Amelia Earhart's true legacy was written in the courage with which she lived. Before her final flight, she left a prophetic letter for her husband: 'Please know that I am quite aware of the hazards. I want to do it because I want to do it. Women must try to do things as men have tried. When they fail, their failure must be but a challenge to others.' Amelia Earhart never grew old; she vanished into the golden sunset of the Pacific, an eternal pioneer of human courage whose spirit flies forever free across the heavens.  Her final letter to her husband stands as a timeless manifesto of human courage, asserting that the pursuit of daring adventure is its own supreme justification. Amelia Earhart's memory continues to inspire millions of women and young girls around the world to break barriers, defy limitations, and reach for the sky.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. Next week, our Top 50 Famous Non-President Americans series continues with Episode 268. Until then, stay curious.
